findings.lens: charismatic non-denominational (Vineyard, Bethel, Hillsong, Third Wave)
findings.claim: The cessationist paragraph attributes the canon-completion argument to all cessationists; many of the best-known ones disown it.
findings.evidence: 'passed away once the apostolic foundation was laid and the New Testament was complete.' Waldron, To Be Continued? (2005) and Schreiner, Spiritual Gifts (2018) argue from the cessation of the apostolate and reject reading 1 Cor 13:10 'the perfect' as the canon. Also 'should be sought' understates 1 Cor 14:1.
findings.fix: '...passed away once the apostolic foundation was laid; many add that the completed Scriptures now do the work those gifts once did.' and, on the continuationist side, 'should be eagerly desired and tested'.

findings.lens: confessional Lutheran (LCMS / WELS / Book of Concord)
findings.claim: The cessationist pole is described only with Warfield's rationale ("authenticated the apostles... New Testament was complete"); Lutheran caution about the gifts rests on a different ground, that the Spirit binds himself to Word and sacrament so that no new revelation is to be expected, and Lutherans do not deny that God still heals in answer to prayer.
findings.evidence: SA III.viii.3-13: "God gives no one his Spirit or grace except through or with the external Word"; whatever is claimed of the Spirit apart from Word and sacrament "is of the devil". LCMS CTCR, The Lutheran Church and the Charismatic Movement (1977): the extraordinary gifts are not to be expected as normative, while refusing to say God cannot work miracles. A Lutheran scoring 75-83 is thus described in words he would not use.
findings.fix: Cessationists hold that the sign gifts authenticated the apostles and their message and passed away once that foundation was laid, or that the Spirit has bound himself to Word and sacrament so that no new revelation is to be expected; God may still heal in answer to prayer, but the gifts of Acts are not the church's ordinary pattern.

findings.claim: "should be sought" is not the Orthodox (or Catholic) view of the gifts, yet the Orthodox coordinate is on the continuationist side; the summary describes only the Pentecostal form of continuance.
findings.evidence: Text: "remain available to the church until Christ returns, and should be sought and tested." Orthodox ascetic teaching warns against seeking visions or gifts as the road to prelest (Ignatius Brianchaninov, The Arena; the Philokalia on discernment); the gifts are received unsought in the lives of the saints; 1 Cor 12:31 is read as pointing to love (Chrysostom, Hom. 32 on 1 Corinthians).
findings.fix: Continuationists hold that the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12, including tongues, prophecy, and healing, remain in the church until Christ returns: Pentecostals and charismatics actively seek them, while Orthodox and Catholics expect them chiefly in the lives of the saints and warn against seeking them; all agree they must be tested.

findings.lens: Pentecostal (Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths)
findings.claim: The continuationist paragraph ('Continuationists hold that the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12, including tongues, prophecy, and healing, remain available to the church until Christ returns, and should be sought and tested') describes the Third Wave position and omits the baptism in the Holy Spirit, which for Pentecostals is the heart of the matter, not the continuation of gifts as such.
findings.evidence: AG Statement of Fundamental Truths art. 7: 'All believers are entitled to and should ardently expect and earnestly seek the promise of the Father, the baptism in the Holy Spirit and fire ... This was the normal experience of all in the early Christian Church'; art. 8 on tongues as initial physical evidence. The summary's 'sought and tested' is acceptable (1 Cor 14:1; 1 Thess 5:21).
findings.fix: Append: 'Pentecostals go further: the baptism in the Holy Spirit is a distinct experience promised to every believer (Acts 2:39), and classical Pentecostal bodies such as the Assemblies of God hold that speaking in tongues is its first sign.'

findings.lens: Presbyterian / Reformed (Westminster Standards, Three Forms of Unity)
findings.claim: The cessationist description ends at 'passed away', with no positive statement, which is the continuationist caricature of cessationism as denying that the Spirit still acts.
findings.evidence: WCF 21.3 and James 5:14-16 prooftexts: Reformed cessationists pray for healing and expect answers; Gaffin and Warfield both distinguish extraordinary gifts from the Spirit's ongoing work through Word, sacrament, prayer and providence.
findings.fix: Append: "...and the New Testament was complete, while the Spirit still works powerfully through Word, sacrament, prayer, and providence."

findings.claim: The cessationist description omits what cessationists affirm, and so invites the caricature that we deny God heals or works miracles today.
findings.evidence: Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles, distinguishes the charismata of the apostolic age from God's ongoing providential and answered-prayer working; LBC 5 (providence) and James 5:14-16 are preached in every cessationist church.
findings.fix: Append to the cessationist sentence: ', while God still heals and acts in answer to prayer and the Spirit's ordinary work of illumination and sanctification continues.'

findings.lens: Reformed charismatic (John Piper, Wayne Grudem, Sam Storms, Sovereign Grace Churches, Acts 29 continuationists)
findings.claim: The cessationist summary's 'and the New Testament was complete' attributes the canon-cessation argument that the strongest cessationist scholars decline.
findings.evidence: Gaffin, Perspectives on Pentecost, and Gaffin in Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? take 1 Corinthians 13:10 as the parousia and rest cessation on the apostolic foundation (Eph 2:20), not on the canon; Waldron, To Be Continued?, likewise. Continuationists win too easily against the canon argument, so it is unfair to the other side.
findings.fix: ...those sign gifts authenticated the apostles and their message, and passed away with them once the church's foundation was laid (Ephesians 2:20).

findings.claim: "passed away once the apostolic foundation was laid and the New Testament was complete" makes the canon reading of 1 Corinthians 13:10 ('the perfect' = completed Scripture) part of the cessationist position as such. Statement 8 correctly says "or"; the summary says "and". The leading academic cessationists explicitly reject the canon reading and hold the foundation argument alone.
findings.evidence: Gaffin, Perspectives on Pentecost (1979), pp. 109-112, reads to teleion as the parousia and disowns the canon interpretation; Warfield never argued from 1 Corinthians 13:10. Popular cessationism (some Strange Fire speakers) does use the canon reading, so it should be marked as a subset, not the definition.
findings.fix: Replace with: "...and passed away once the apostolic foundation was laid; some add that this coincided with the completion of the New Testament."
